sections.title: The idea

blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: Your PDFs do not cover this topic, so this page was written for the site. Your 12-week plan lists React, hooks, rendering, performance, state management and TypeScript. Check it against the official documentation, or give me a PDF to replace it.

blocks: React's core idea fits in one line: **UI = f(state)**. You describe what the screen should look like for the current state, and React works out the DOM changes. You never tell it "add this row".

sections.title: Components, JSX and props
blocks: A component is a function that returns JSX. JSX compiles to function calls, so it is JavaScript, not a template language: `{}` holds any expression. Props are the function's read-only arguments.

blocks.title: Props down, events up

walkthrough.title: Props
walkthrough.text: A component receives data and callbacks as read-only props.

walkthrough.title: Conditional rendering
walkthrough.text: JSX holds expressions, so a ternary picks what to show.

walkthrough.title: Events go up
walkthrough.text: The child does not change the data. It calls the callback, and the owner of the state decides.

walkthrough.title: Lists need keys
walkthrough.text: `key` tells React which row is which between renders. Use a stable id.

blocks.title: One-way data flow
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  P[Parent owns the state] -->|props: data and callbacks| C[Child renders them]
  C -->|calls the callback on a click| P
  P -->|state changes, parent re-renders| P
blocks.caption: Data flows down through props; events flow up through callbacks.

sections.title: State and re-rendering
blocks: State is memory that survives between renders. Calling the setter schedules a new render, and React calls your function again with the new value.
State is treated as immutable: create a new object or array. React compares by reference, so mutating in place and setting the same reference causes no re-render.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Do not use the array index as `key` when a list can be reordered or filtered. React will reuse the wrong component instance, and state such as input text ends up on the wrong row.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: **What is the virtual DOM?** React keeps a lightweight description of the UI. On each render it compares the new tree with the old one (reconciliation) and applies only the differences to the real DOM. The benefit is mainly the programming model, describing the result instead of the steps, not raw speed.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- UI is a function of state.
- Props are read-only; events go up through callbacks.
- Never mutate state: create new objects and arrays.
- List keys must be stable ids, not indexes.

items.question: Why doesn't `items.push(x); setItems(items)` re-render?
items.answer: It is the same array reference, and React skips the update when the value is identical. Create a new array.

items.question: Why is an array index a bad `key`?
items.answer: When items are inserted, removed or reordered, the index maps to a different item, so React reuses the wrong instance and its state.

items.question: Where should state live if two sibling components need it?
items.answer: In their closest common parent, passed down as props. This is called lifting state up.
